title: LinkedIn Premium Pricing (2026): Which Plan Makes Sense for B2B Prospecting?
summary: LinkedIn Premium pricing in 2026: compare Career, Business, All-in-One, and Sales Navigator costs, features, and the right plan for B2B prospecting.
body_markdown:
*Pricing reviewed October 16, 2026. USD starting prices are estimates; verify the live offer shown in your account before buying.*


## LinkedIn Premium pricing at a glance


Start with the prospecting task, not the subscription name. A seller maintaining a known network has a different buying decision from one repeatedly building new account lists. The prices below establish the budget; the remaining question is which paid capability, if any, your current workflow actually needs.

These are LinkedIn's listed USD starting estimates, not a guaranteed checkout quote. LinkedIn says pricing can vary by billing frequency, promotion, tax, device, country, and time. A plan's name or a feature listed somewhere on a comparison page does not establish that the feature is included in every tier. Check the live plan comparison and checkout details for your account, especially before purchasing for a team.


A useful first distinction: Career and Business are broad professional subscriptions, All-in-One combines several small-business jobs, and Sales Navigator is the dedicated prospecting product. If you only need ordinary networking, start by asking whether a paid subscription solves a specific recurring problem that your free account does not.


## What the plans actually buy


### Premium Career: pay for a job-search workflow


Career is intended for people looking for work or developing their careers. LinkedIn lists job-search and profile tools, access to profile-view information, and **five InMail messages per month** . Its listed USD starting price is $39.99 monthly or $239.88 annually. The annual amount is the stated price, not a promise that every account will see the same checkout offer.


It is not the natural choice for a B2B seller just because it includes InMail. The product is organized around finding roles, improving applications, and contacting hiring managers or recruiters. If your business use case is identifying buying accounts and decision-makers, compare Business and Sales Navigator instead.


### Premium Business: broader reach, not a sales intelligence system


LinkedIn positions Premium Business for professionals who want to build a network, strengthen their profile, and pursue business goals. The comparison page lists a starting price of $69.99 per month and describes profile credibility, networking and communication capabilities, and features intended to support professional visibility. It is a plausible fit for a founder or consultant who spends meaningful time building a personal brand and keeping professional conversations moving.


Business can support finding people and companies as well as networking. The upgrade question is whether you need a repeatable sales-search workflow rather than ordinary lookups: a defined account segment, specific buyer roles, a timing filter and a way to revisit matching prospects. The worked comparison below separates that workflow from a known-company lookup, without treating search access as evidence of sales results.


### Premium All-in-One: an option for small-business generalists


At a listed starting price of $89.99 monthly, All-in-One targets small-business owners who combine selling, marketing, and hiring rather than working in specialist teams. LinkedIn describes prospect suggestions and insights alongside promotional and job-posting credits. Its comparison page lists **30 InMail credits monthly** for this plan.


The bundled scope may be useful if you will actually use the mix. It may be poor value if your only job is prospecting and you need a more structured way to search, prioritize, and monitor accounts. Conversely, a sales team should not assume All-in-One is a lower-cost substitute for Sales Navigator's specialized sales functions. Review the current comparison page and any limits attached to the credits or features before treating the bundle as a fit.


### Sales Navigator: specialized prospecting capabilities


LinkedIn describes Sales Navigator as a sales tool for finding buyers, understanding buying groups, and engaging at relevant moments. Its comparison page highlights more than 50 sales-specialized search filters, account and lead insights, buyer signals and alerts, and **50 monthly InMail credits** . The product family also includes features such as TeamLink, relationship mapping, SmartLinks, team collaboration, and CRM-related workflows, but availability depends on the plan and may have conditions. Do not assume that Core includes every item on the family-level feature page.


Core starts at $119.99 monthly or $1,079.88 annually per license. Advanced starts at $159.99 monthly or $1,799.88 annually per license. Advanced Plus is quote-based. These are not interchangeable labels for one package: review the live plan comparison against the actual workflow you need, including CRM support, team management, and integrations. If you are one seller, Core may be the tier to evaluate first; if you need team-level coordination or deeper CRM workflows, confirm the specific tier and purchase route with LinkedIn before budgeting.


## Premium Business vs. Sales Navigator for B2B prospecting


Use LinkedIn's published allowances to narrow the choice: Premium Business lists 15 InMail credits a month, All-in-One 30, and Sales Navigator 50 across Core, Advanced and Advanced Plus. Navigator also lists more than 50 sales-specialized search filters. These are documented product differences, not evidence that an upgrade will produce more meetings.

Business already supports people and company search. If your task is “find the VP of Sales at these named companies,” start with the company and title search you already have. Premium Business is not unable to find buyers, and a search-volume constraint is different from needing sales-specific filters. Do not pay for Core merely because your contacts are prospective customers.


Now change the task: “Find US sales leaders at software companies with 51–200 employees, narrow to people who changed jobs, and revisit that segment for new matches.” In Sales Navigator, use Account Search for industry, headquarters and company headcount, save the matching accounts, then use Lead Search for the account list, geography, function or title, seniority, and Changed Jobs. Save the lead search to receive notifications of new matching results. The criteria are an invented buyer brief; this is a documented workflow, not a search we ran or a measured customer result.


LinkedIn’s Core account-types description explicitly includes advanced search and saved leads/accounts. Its search-filter page and usage guide document the named filters and saved-search workflow. That makes Core the first tier to evaluate for this recurring segmentation job, not Advanced just because it has more features. Confirm the named filters and notifications in your actual Core offer before buying. This comparison does not establish that Business cannot locate the same people through ordinary searches and manual profile checks, or that every Navigator feature is included in Core.


The buying decision is therefore narrower than “Business for networking, Navigator for sales.” For the known-company lookup, keep free access if it suffices; evaluate Business if its search access or profile tools solve a recurring constraint. For the recurring multi-criterion segment, evaluate Core against the exact steps above and compare the manual work it would replace. One unambiguous allowance boundary: if the job requires 20 new InMail credits in a month, Business’s 15-credit allowance falls short and Core’s 50 covers that count. Existing credits and actual messaging terms still matter; this is not a recommendation to send 20 messages. At the listed monthly rates Core costs $50 more than Business. That buys a different toolset and allowance, not proven meetings or revenue.


InMail can be a useful bridge to someone outside your existing network, but message credits are not a prospecting strategy by themselves. A larger allowance does not establish that a recipient is relevant, that the timing is right, or that the message deserves a response. Likewise, don't compare InMail counts without considering the surrounding tools: search, account context, buying-group information, team collaboration, and CRM support can be more consequential than the raw allowance.


Sales Navigator is strongest when its dedicated search and sales context address a real limitation in how you work. LinkedIn's professional graph, identity, and network context are meaningful advantages: sellers can use shared connections, professional profiles, and the platform's own signals in one environment. That can be especially helpful when reaching people where they already maintain a professional presence. A separate research process should complement that access, not pretend to replace it.


Neither upgrade is automatic. If you have a short list of accounts and rarely prospect, a paid plan may sit unused. If your target market is narrow and your free account already supports the work, pay only when you can point to a concrete recurring constraint. If a team needs CRM sync or centralized administration, validate those exact requirements rather than relying on a broad “Sales Navigator” claim.


## Calculate the cost beyond the subscription


The subscription fee is only one part of the cost. Also account for the time spent selecting accounts, validating whether they fit, finding the right contact, preparing a relevant reason to reach out, following up, recording outcomes, and maintaining data responsibly. These tasks still exist whether a rep does them manually or uses separate tools.


A simple way to assess value is to document a representative week before purchasing. Count how many hours go to prospect discovery and qualification, how many accounts become plausible opportunities, and where the process stalls. Then estimate the subscription's annual cost using the actual checkout price and seats required. For a monthly plan, multiply the displayed monthly rate by the number of paid months; for annual billing, use the amount LinkedIn shows rather than assuming a discount. Add any taxes and related tool or administration costs. Do not treat a lower annualized price as a saving if you may cancel before using the full term.


At the listed USD starting rates, twelve monthly Core payments total $1,439.88; the listed annual payment is $1,079.88, a $360 difference before taxes and account-specific offers. Those figures compare Core with Core, not Business with Core. A lower annual total commits more money up front: verify the cancellation and refund terms before choosing annual billing.


Next, define the outcome you expect from the missing capability. For example: reduce time spent locating decision-makers, identify more appropriate accounts, or give a team a consistent way to follow signals. Set a review date and use a small, comparable sample of work to see whether the feature changed the process. Avoid promising a revenue return from a subscription price alone. Results depend on the market, offer, data quality, timing, and execution, not just software access.


Sales Navigator helps identify prospects on LinkedIn. Account qualification still requires a reason to approach a particular company now, such as a relevant hiring push or an expansion that creates demand for what you sell. Check that reason before writing the message. A separate outbound product does not grant LinkedIn subscription features; assess its account research and execution separately from your LinkedIn plan.


## A practical decision checklist


Use this sequence before upgrading:


1.


**Name the job.** Is the goal job search, broader networking, small-business generalist work, or dedicated B2B prospecting? Choose the product category that matches, not the one with the most attractive headline feature.


2.


**Write down the constraint.** “Need more InMail” is incomplete. Specify whether you need search depth, account context, alerts, team collaboration, or simply more time for research.


3.


**Test the free option first.** If your current LinkedIn account handles your actual volume and workflow, keep it. A paid tier is not a requirement for having professional conversations.


4.


**Verify the exact tier.** Compare the current feature list with your use case. For Sales Navigator, confirm Core, Advanced, or Advanced Plus availability for every required capability, including CRM and team functions.


5.


**Compare real total costs.** Use the price shown at checkout, billing frequency, number of seats, taxes, and cancellation terms. Don't project a feature to every plan when LinkedIn has not clearly assigned it.


6.


**Set a measurable review.** Decide what should improve and when you will assess it. If the subscription does not change the work, reconsider at renewal.


For most B2B sellers, the decision is not “Premium or nothing.” It is whether their bottleneck is LinkedIn access and prospecting tools, or the research and qualification work that happens around those tools. Keep LinkedIn if its network and discovery capabilities are central to reaching your buyers. Consider Sales Navigator when its specialized search and sales context solve a repeatable problem. Consider a separate research and outbound workflow only when prioritizing accounts and establishing relevant reasons to contact them is the gap.


If account research and qualification are the bottleneck after you have decided how LinkedIn fits your sales process,[book a Coldreach demo](https://airtable.com/app6J50ppnP1E86QV/pagToOMvuy00fPqNt/form) to see whether its research-driven outbound workflow is relevant. It complements LinkedIn access; it is not a substitute for a LinkedIn subscription.


## FAQs


### How much does LinkedIn Premium cost?


The listed USD starting prices reviewed October 16, 2026 are $39.99/month for Career, $69.99/month for Business, $89.99/month for All-in-One, and $119.99/month for Sales Navigator Core. Confirm the live account-specific price, billing terms, tax, and offers before purchase.


### Is annual billing cheaper?


LinkedIn lists Career at $239.88/year, Sales Navigator Core at $1,079.88/year, and Advanced at $1,799.88/year. The cited official comparison says Core annual billing saves 25% and Advanced saves 6% versus monthly pricing. Annual prices for Business and All-in-One were not confirmed in the source reviewed here.


### How many InMail messages do the plans include?


The official comparison lists five per month for Career, 15 for Premium Business, 30 for All-in-One, and 50 for Sales Navigator. Check the plan page and checkout for your region and current account terms.


### Is Premium Business the same as Sales Navigator?


No. Business is aimed at broader networking and professional visibility. Sales Navigator is LinkedIn's specialized prospecting product, with sales-focused search and account capabilities. Confirm which Navigator features belong to the tier you are considering.


### Can I try a plan and cancel?


Trial eligibility and cancellation terms can vary by plan, region, and account. Before starting, check whether a payment method is required, the renewal date and price, the cancellation deadline, and when cancellation takes effect. Do not rely on a generic trial banner as the complete terms.
